cues.text: Begin with the dorsiventral leaf in transverse section.
A labels the upper epidermis.
B points to the elongated palisade mesophyll beneath it.
C indicates the more loosely arranged spongy mesophyll, with intercellular air
spaces.
These are tissue regions rather than three different organs.
The drawing is a typical teaching model and does not show every chloroplast,
cell wall or cuticular detail.
Both palisade and spongy tissues can contribute to photosynthesis.
Do not infer that an empty looking space is a missing cell that must be
filled:
intercellular spaces support gas movement within the leaf.
Use cell arrangement together with position to recognise each region.
Trace the selected leaf bundle.
X identifies xylem toward the upper, or adaxial, side, while P identifies
phloem toward the lower, or abaxial, side.
An enclosing outline represents the bundle sheath.
D points to a selected stomatal opening in the lower epidermis.
Many typical dorsiventral leaves have more stomata on the lower surface, but
this simplified sketch cannot establish that every dicot leaf has stomata only
below.
The gap is a simplified stomatal opening, not a complete guard cell drawing.
Do not transfer a stem's centre to outside labels directly onto a leaf without
first identifying its upper and lower surfaces.
Now examine the grass leaf model.
A points to a group of enlarged bulliform cells in the upper epidermis.
The mesophyll is not divided into the distinct palisade and spongy regions
shown in the preceding diagram.
Selected stomatal gaps appear on both surfaces, and bundle sheaths surround
the
two illustrated vascular bundles.
These features support the familiar isobilateral grass leaf comparison.
They do not mean that every monocot leaf has identical anatomy or perfectly
identical upper and lower surfaces.
Only selected cells and bundles are drawn.
The transverse section does not directly show parallel venation, which
requires
a different view of the leaf.
Use the grass model to connect structure and water status.
When bulliform cells are turgid, the leaf blade is exposed.
Loss of water and turgor in these cells can contribute to inward rolling of
the
blade, reducing its exposed surface.
This is a familiar grass adaptation, not a claim that bulliform cells actively
pump the entire leaf shut like a muscle.
The static diagram shows their location but does not measure the rate of water
loss or the exact rolling angle.
Xylem and phloem retain the upper and lower orientation shown within each
selected bundle.
Explain the mechanism without treating a schematic as an experiment.
Move to the secondary growth board.
A represents an early dicot stem with six selected bundles.
Solid marks indicate fascicular cambium within bundles, between their phloem
and xylem.
Dashed marks indicate intervening regions where interfascicular cambium
develops.
Their continuity produces the vascular cambium ring represented at B.
The model is a developmental comparison rather than two annual rings.
Cortex, epidermis and many cell details are omitted.
A root can also form vascular cambium, but its developmental origin is not
simply identical to the stem sequence shown here.
Establish the organ before memorising where a cambium arises.
In B, C labels the vascular cambium ring.
X marks secondary xylem inside it and P secondary phloem outside it.
Vascular cambium is a lateral meristem, and its activity increases stem girth.
Secondary xylem forms wood; the word secondary describes developmental origin
rather than a second, inferior transport system.
The drawing's circular boundaries separate tissue zones and are not a count of
annual growth rings.
Older primary tissues are omitted for clarity, so do not assume the entire
inner region began as secondary xylem.
Keep product direction, tissue identity and developmental stage separate when
interpreting the diagram.
Panel A of the final board is an outside to inside strip through periderm.
Cork is on the outside.
The thick line represents phellogen, or cork cambium, and phelloderm lies
inside it.
These three components together form periderm.
Cork cells typically become dead and suberised, while phelloderm is living
parenchymatous tissue.
Do not confuse cork cambium with vascular cambium: they produce different
tissues.
Periderm is not the whole bark.
In the broad anatomical use, bark includes tissues outside the vascular
cambium, including secondary phloem and periderm.
The simplified strip does not show every layer that can occur in an older
stem.
Panel B compares parts of one simplified secondary xylem increment.
The inner, older part is early wood, illustrated with larger vessel lumens.
The outer, younger part is late wood, illustrated with smaller lumens.
This is a selected comparison, not a scale drawing of every woody species.
In a regular yearly seasonal cycle, early and late wood together form one
annual growth ring, not two years.
False rings or missing rings can complicate an age estimate, so a few
concentric lines alone are insufficient.
Heartwood and sapwood are a different distinction from early and late wood;
their boundaries are not supplied by this board.
